headline: With in-person early voting over nearly everywhere, the official same-point comparison across five states still implies a national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2) against 2022 and about D+3.9 (±1.3) against 2024 (four states), while the polls say D+8.9 and the app's forecast D+6.9: in the Nov 1 files Florida is R+2.5 by registration on 5.40 million ballots against R+6.2 at two days out in 2022, Nevada D+6.3 against D+1.3, Colorado D+6.7 against D+3.2, Iowa's absentee pool D+9.7 against D+19.8 and Pennsylvania's mail D+39.5 against D+48.6. The finals elsewhere lean Democratic: Jon Ralston has Nevada's Democrats up just over 43,000 ballots (just under 6 points) with a record midterm Clark County firewall near 66,000, North Carolina closed at 2,816,821 early ballots (35.7% of registered voters, D 38%, unaffiliated 35%, R 26%, against R 31% in 2022), Georgia at 2,810,170 (+13% on 2022, with 883,000 Democratic-primary voters to 644,000 Republican-primary voters), and Texas at a record 7.7 million; but Republicans won the closing days in Florida and Texas, Pennsylvania's mail returns trail 2022 by 5%, and Arizona's ballots are R+12,335 on Go Right Strategies' count.

measures.aff: Official data. 5,402,758 ballots in the Nov 1 file (mail 1,937,212, in person 3,465,546) vs. the state's figures at two days out in 2024; 2024 is a presidential baseline in which Republicans had moved to in-person voting. Against 2022 the same file reads R+2.5 vs. R+6.2

measures.aff: Official data. 718,903 ballots through Oct 31's file (mail 410,884, in person 308,019) vs. Ralston's count at three days out in 2024 (Republicans up 4.0); 2022 at the same point was D+1.3

measures.label: Colorado: returned ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin
measures.src: Colorado Secretary of State daily ballot-return release via the app's official comparison, Nov 1
measures.aff: Official data. 1,591,323 ballots through Nov 1 vs. 2,092,035 at two days out in 2024; 2022 at the same point was D+3.2

measures.label: Iowa: absentee ballots received by registration, D-minus-R margin
measures.src: Iowa Secretary of State daily absentee report via the app's official comparison, Oct 31
measures.aff: Official data. 147,027 absentee ballots received in the Oct 31 report vs. the state's report at the same point in 2024; 2022 at the same point was D+19.8, and Iowa Democrats vote absentee far more than Republicans in every year

measures.src: Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Nov 1
measures.aff: Official data. 1,056,549 ballots returned through Nov 1 (of 1,297,730 requested) vs. 1,739,606 at two days out in 2024; no in-person early voting, and the mail pool is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+48.6 at this point in 2022)

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024. Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania are computed from the state files by the update job (Florida 5,402,758 ballots in the Nov 1 file against the state's 2024 figures at two days out; Nevada 718,903 through Oct 31 against Ralston's 2024 count; Colorado 1,591,323 through Nov 1; Iowa 147,027 absentees in the Oct 31 report; Pennsylvania 1,056,549 mail ballots through Nov 1); Maine is Call the Map's reading of the state file (211,791 ballots through Oct 26). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida most of all because 2024's Republicans had moved to in-person early voting; against 2022 the official comparison is narrower and mixed (Florida R+2.5 vs. R+6.2, Nevada D+6.3 vs. D+1.3, Colorado D+6.7 vs. D+3.2, Iowa D+9.7 vs. D+19.8, Pennsylvania D+39.5 vs. D+48.6), and North Carolina's comparison is computed from the State Board's files.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 covers five states and implies a national vote of about D-0.8, unchanged through the final week; against 2024 it reads about D+3.9 on four states.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Nov 1 file counts 5,402,758 ballots at R+2.5 (mail 830,632 Democrats to 677,817 Republicans; in person 1,209,843 to 1,497,201), against R+6.2 at two days out in 2022; Nevada's 718,903 ballots in the Oct 31 file are D+6.3 (mail D+54,099, in person R+8,674) against D+1.3 at the same point in 2022; Colorado's 1,591,323 returned ballots are D+6.7 against D+3.2; Iowa's 147,027 absentees are D+9.7 against D+19.8; and Pennsylvania's 1,056,549 returned mail ballots are D+39.5 against D+48.6. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +3.1, +4.2, +3.0, -2.2 and -2.0 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2), against polls at D+8.9 and the app's forecast at D+6.9. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Florida R+2.5 against R+10.6 (worth about +6.8), Nevada D+6.3 against R+4.0 (+8.7), Colorado D+6.7 against D+1.9 (+4.1) and Arizona's county compilation at R+0.8 on 1,602,837 ballots against R+8.4 (+6.4) pool to about D+3.9 (±1.3); Pennsylvania's mail at D+39.5 against D+23.0 is worth about +3.7 (±3.5) and Iowa's D+9.7 against R+1.2 about +2.4 (±3.3). Arizona has a 2024 baseline but none for 2022.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Nov 1
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 31)
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Nov 1
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 4, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats lead by just over 43,000 ballots (just under 6 points) after early voting, with a record midterm Clark County firewall near 66,000 and Washoe County D+5; Ralston says Republicans would need a 2022-style Election Day to erase it.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's 9 a.m. Nov 1 entry: Democrats are ahead by 'just over 43,000 ballots,' just under 6 percent, with about 500 more in unaccepted mail; the Clark firewall is 'a few ballots under 66,000,' almost 13.5 percent; Washoe, a Republican county by 3 points in registration, has a 5-point Democratic ballot advantage; the rurals are R+30,000; mail is 58 percent of the statewide total; turnout is just under 730,000, about 35 percent of active voters, with 300,000 to 350,000 ballots still to come. Republicans would need about 194,097 Election Day ballots breaking like 2022's (R+22.2) to erase the lead, against 215,517 Election Day ballots cast in 2022, and 'at least 30,000 and maybe more' extra Election Day ballots to save the governor's race. His Oct 31 entry called the 65,000 Clark firewall a midterm record, above 2012's 71,000 and 2016's 73,000 presidential-year levels in proportion but short of 2020's roughly 81,000. The state's Oct 31 file reads D+6.3 on 718,903 ballots against D+1.3 at this point in 2022 and R+4.0 in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 31)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina closed early voting at a record 2,816,821 ballots, 35.7% of registered voters, with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022 and Black voters' ballots 1.5 times 2022's.
bullets.html: WBTV's reading of the NC FreeEnterprise Foundation tracker (Nov 1): 2,816,821 early ballots, 35.7% of registered voters against 29.0% turnout in 2022's early period; Democrats 38% ('steady'), unaffiliated 35% (30% in 2022), Republicans 26% (31% in 2022); turnout above 2022 in 97 of 100 counties; Black voters nearly 600,000 ballots, '1.5x' 2022; voters 18-25 more than 200,000, nearly double. Michael Bitzer (Nov 1): 2.8 million early ballots, about 36% of registered voters; mail accepted 92,395, about 3.3%; 46% of registered Democrats have voted, 32% ahead of their 2022 numbers, unaffiliated voters nearly 1 million, up 52%, Republicans up 9% on 2022; on his assumptions the early vote is about 55% Democratic to 38% Republican, Republicans would need about 58% of the remaining registrants for a tie, and the electorate looks 'more like 2018 than 2022.' Call the Map: D+12.2 against D+6.8 at the same point in 2022, ballots up 31%. The app's own file carries the official comparison (2,819,922 accepted ballots through Nov 1).
sources: Michael Bitzer, Center for NC Politics, Nov 1
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Bitzer is a nonpartisan academic; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Georgia finished at 2,810,170 ballots, 13% above 2022's early vote, with Democratic-primary voters outnumbering Republican-primary voters 883,000 to 644,000 and the Black share up to 32.4%.
bullets.html: Secretary of State figures (Atlanta News First, Oct 30): 2,810,170 ballots, 2,691,841 in person and 118,329 absentee, 37.3% of registered voters; 2022's in-person midterm record was nearly 2.3 million and its overall early record about 2.5 million. The AJC (Oct 31): more than 2.8 million, up 13% on the 2022 midterm; mail and electronic ballots 4.2% of the early vote against nearly 9% in 2022; white voters 52.6% of ballots against 58.2% 'at this point in 2022,' Black voters 32.4% against 30.2% (and 26.8% at the same stage of 2024), Hispanic 3.7% against 2%; voters 18-29 11%, voters 50 and over nearly 65%; 883,000-plus Democratic-primary voters against about 644,000 Republican-primary voters; Harris-strong precincts cast about 60,000 more early ballots than Trump-strong precincts, where 2022's gap was about 1,000; more than 630,000 early voters skipped 2022 and more than 435,000 2022 Election Day voters voted early; about 1.9 million registered voters in Trump strongholds and 1.8 million in Harris strongholds had not voted.
sources: Atlanta Journal-Constitution (Greg Bluestein and Charles Minshew), Oct 31
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; Georgia has no party registration, so party is primary history

bullets.title: Texas: a record 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% of registered voters, against 5.5 million in 2022; Republican-primary voters finished ahead of Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots, 2,238,247 to 2,100,396.
bullets.html: The Texas Tribune (Nov 1, preliminary): more than 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% turnout, past 2018's record; 2022's early vote was 5.5 million (31%) and 2024's 9 million (49%); registration above 19 million, up 2.2% on November 2024. The Secretary of State's count as of Friday Oct 30 was 7,410,631, 38.92% of 19,041,684 registered voters (CBS Texas). theoelections (as of Oct 30): 7,744,549 early ballots, 7,463,553 in person and 280,996 by mail; in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 2,238,247 (30.0%) against Democratic-primary-only voters' 2,100,396 (28.1%), both 185,982 (2.5%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%); the mail runs 32.8% Democratic-only (92,275) to 26.2% Republican-only (73,688). At the same point in 2022 Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 on Derek Ryan's count (NBC 5, Oct 27). Mark Jones: 'We're not going to hit presidential levels, but this is definitely high turnout'; Democratic strategist Matt Angle: 'That doesn't mean Democrats are going to win.'
sources: Texas Tribune (Colleen Deguzman) via KSAT, Nov 1
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; theoelections is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

bullets.title: Florida: R+2.5 in the Nov 1 file after nearly 1.4 million weekend ballots, with Republicans up 287,000 in person and Democrats up 153,000 by mail; turnout is about 300,000 ahead of 2022's same point.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Nov 1 file (the app's official comparison) has 3,465,546 in-person ballots, 1,497,201 Republican to 1,209,843 Democratic (R+287,358), and 1,937,212 mail ballots returned, 830,632 Democratic to 677,817 Republican (D+152,815): 40.3% Republican to 37.8% Democratic on 5,402,758 ballots, from R+1.8 on Oct 29, R+1.0 on Oct 27 and D+6.7 at twenty days out. Bay News 9 (Nov 2): 'just under 5.2 million' ballots at Sunday's close, 'nearly 300,000 more votes than at the same point during the 2022 midterms,' with almost 1.4 million cast Friday through Sunday; Republicans more than 1.4 million in person and just over 668,000 by mail, Democrats just over 1.1 million in person and more than 800,000 by mail, no-party voters nearly 700,000. At two days out in 2022 the state was R+6.2, and at the same point in 2024 R+10.6.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Nov 1
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 4, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Wisconsin's absentees are about 50,000 ahead of 2022's same point with mail down and in-person up, Michigan passed 1.8 million, Pennsylvania's mail is 5% behind 2022 and Arizona is R+12,335.
bullets.html: Wisconsin (WPR, Elections Commission data as of Oct 30): 693,334 absentee ballots returned, 'about 50,000 more than at the same point in 2022'; mail about 300,000 against about 384,000 in 2022, in-person about 394,000 against about 259,000; Milwaukee's mail down more than 25% and in-person up 45%, Dane's mail down more than 30% and in-person up about 50%, Washington's in-person up about 75%, Waukesha's up more than 40%. Michigan: more than 1.8 million had voted as of Friday Oct 30 (AP), after 1.3 million absentee and 358,000 early in-person ballots on Friday's dashboard (CBS Detroit). Pennsylvania (Call the Map, state file through Oct 31): 1,053,168 mail ballots returned, 5% below the same point in 2022, Democrats 681,934 (down 12% from 771,898), Republicans 265,272 (up 14% from 233,284), D+39.6 against D+48.6; the state's Nov 1 file has 1,056,549 returned of 1,297,730 requested. Arizona (Go Right Strategies' county compilation, Nov 1): 1,602,707 ballots, Republicans 609,283 (38.0%), Democrats 596,948 (37.2%), other 396,476, R+12,335; Maricopa R+5,314, Pima D+55,007. Colorado: 1,591,323 ballots through Nov 1 at D+6.7 (the app's panel). Maine: 275,563 absentees returned by Oct 29 against more than 202,000 at the same point in 2022 (WGME).
sources: WPR (Avery Martinez) via Urban Milwaukee, Oct 31
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets and an independent tracker; Go Right Strategies is a Republican consulting firm

bullets.title: Nationally, 54.5 million have voted, past 2022's 45.9 million; registered Democrats are 43% of ballots in the party-registration states and Republicans 32%, and the party gap moved toward Republicans in three of Call the Map's five compared states.
bullets.html: UF Election Lab counted 54,467,368 ballots across 49 reporting jurisdictions in the app's Nov 2 file (24,429,766 by mail, 30,147,504 in person), against 45,920,446 early votes in all of 2022. Newsweek (Oct 31, from UF Election Lab's Friday figures): about 49.6 million early votes, 22.9 million by mail and 26.8 million in person; in the states that report party registration, Democrats 43%, Republicans 32%, others 25%; the AP found 50% more Texans voted early than in 2022 and South Carolina's early vote up 83%. Call the Map (Nov 1): 51,430,902 ballots in 47 states; the five states comparable day by day with 2022 (North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Maine, Nevada and Florida) are up 14% together, four of five ahead of 2022's pace, and 'the registered party gap moved toward Republicans' in three of the five (Pennsylvania, Maine and Nevada's Clark mail) and toward Democrats in North Carolina and Florida. DDHQ's Geoffrey Skelley (Nov 1): North Carolina's registration margin among early voters swung about 13 points toward Democrats against the same point in 2024, but 'we must be careful not to divine with certainty winners and losers from the entrails of AB/EV data.'
sources: Decision Desk HQ, The Bellwether (Geoffrey Skelley), Nov 1
bullets.aff: McDonald's lab is nonpartisan; Call the Map is an independent tracker; Decision Desk HQ is a nonpartisan firm

calendar_note: In-person early voting has ended in Georgia, Texas, Nevada and Arizona (Oct 30), North Carolina, South Carolina and Kentucky (Oct 31), Florida, Michigan, Wisconsin and Ohio (Nov 1); Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota and Nebraska close Nov 2. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting; Pennsylvania's mail ballots must reach county offices by 8 p.m. Nov 3. Polls close Nov 3 from 6 p.m. ET (Indiana, Kentucky) to midnight (Alaska).
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 49 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 26-Nov 1) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania) implies a national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2), unchanged through the final week: in the Nov 1 files Florida is R+2.5 by registration against R+6.2 at two days out in 2022, Nevada D+6.3 against D+1.3, Colorado D+6.7 against D+3.2, Iowa's absentee pool D+9.7 against D+19.8 and Pennsylvania's mail D+39.5 against D+48.6; against 2024, Florida (R+2.5 vs. R+10.6), Nevada (D+6.3 vs. R+4.0), Colorado (D+6.7 vs. D+1.9) and Arizona (R+0.8 vs. R+8.4) pool to about D+3.9 (±1.3), so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls that have moved to D+8.9. The final tallies in the states without party registration lean Democratic: Ralston has Nevada's Democrats up just over 43,000 ballots with a record midterm Clark firewall near 66,000 and Washoe D+5, North Carolina closed at 2,816,821 ballots with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022, and Georgia's 2,810,170 ballots include 883,000 Democratic-primary voters to 644,000 Republican-primary voters; but Republicans won the closing days in Florida (R+2.5 from R+1.0 on Oct 27) and Texas (Republican-primary voters 2,238,247 to 2,100,396 among in-person ballots), Pennsylvania's mail is 5% behind 2022 with Democratic returns down 12%, and Arizona is R+12,335. The remaining tests are Election Day itself: whether Republicans' Election Day margins match 2022's (Ralston says they would need about 194,000 Election Day ballots breaking R+22 to erase Nevada's lead; Bitzer says they would need about 58% of North Carolina's remaining registrants), and how many of Pennsylvania's 241,000 outstanding mail ballots arrive by 8 p.m.

signals.title: Nevada's Democrats finished early voting up just over 43,000 ballots (just under 6 points), with a record midterm Clark County firewall near 66,000 and Washoe County D+5
signals.value: Jon Ralston, 9 a.m. Nov 1: Democrats lead by 'just over 43,000 ballots,' just under 6 percent, plus about 500 in unaccepted mail; Clark's firewall is 'a few ballots under 66,000' (almost 13.5 percent); Washoe, R+3 in registration, is D+5 in ballots; rurals R+30,000; mail 58 percent of the total; turnout just under 730,000 (about 35 percent of actives), with 300,000-350,000 to come. Oct 31: the 65,000 Clark firewall is a midterm record; 75.1% of 2022's Democratic voters, 58.9% of its Republicans and 51.6% of its nonpartisans had voted, with about 135,800 Republican 2022 voters outstanding.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. Republicans would need about 194,097 Election Day ballots breaking like 2022's R+22.2 to erase the lead (2022 had 215,517 Election Day ballots), and 'at least 30,000 and maybe more' extra Election Day ballots to save the governor's race; the rurals usually give Republicans 55,000-60,000. The state's Oct 31 file reads D+6.3 on 718,903 ballots against D+1.3 at this point in 2022 and R+4.0 in 2024 (the app's official panel).
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: North Carolina's final early vote is 2,816,821 ballots, 35.7% of registered voters, with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022, Democrats 38% and Black voters' ballots 1.5 times 2022's
signals.value: WBTV (Nov 1, NC FreeEnterprise Foundation tracker): 2,816,821 early ballots, 35.7% of registered voters against 29.0% in 2022; Democrats 38%, unaffiliated 35% (30% in 2022), Republicans 26% (31%); turnout above 2022 in 97 of 100 counties; Black voters nearly 600,000, '1.5x' 2022; 18-25 more than 200,000, nearly double. Bitzer (Nov 1): 46% of registered Democrats have voted, 32% ahead of 2022; unaffiliated nearly 1 million, up 52%; Republicans up 9%; mail 92,395 (3.3%). Call the Map: D+12.2 against D+6.8 at the same point in 2022, ballots up 31%.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice; much of the surge is 2022 Election Day voters moving earlier, and Republicans outvoted Democrats on Election Day 2022. Bitzer's 55-38 modeled split rests on his assumptions (D 95/5, R 90/10, UNA 50/39), and he expects about 1.5 million more votes. The app's own file carries the official comparison.
signals.src: WBTV, Nov 1; Center for NC Politics (Michael Bitzer), Nov 1; Call the Map, Nov 1
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Bitzer is a nonpartisan academic; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Georgia's 2,810,170 early ballots are 13% above 2022's, with Democratic-primary voters ahead of Republican-primary voters 883,000 to 644,000 and the Black share 32.4% against 30.2% at this point in 2022
signals.value: Secretary of State figures (Atlanta News First, Oct 30): 2,810,170 ballots, 2,691,841 in person and 118,329 absentee, 37.3% of registered voters; 2022's overall early record was about 2.5 million. AJC (Oct 31): up 13% on 2022; white voters 52.6% against 58.2% 'at this point in 2022,' Black 32.4% against 30.2% (26.8% at the same stage of 2024), Hispanic 3.7% against 2%; 883,000-plus Democratic-primary voters to about 644,000 Republican-primary voters; Harris-strong precincts cast about 60,000 more ballots than Trump-strong precincts, against a gap of about 1,000 in 2022; more than 630,000 early voters skipped 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration: primary history covers only some voters and the precinct comparison is to 2024's presidential vote. The electorate is old (voters 50 and over nearly 65%), mail is down to 4.2% of the early vote, and about 1.9 million registered voters in Trump strongholds had not voted against 1.8 million in Harris strongholds.
signals.src: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Oct 31; Atlanta News First, Oct 30

signals.title: Texas's record 7.7 million early votes (40.5% of registered voters) are 2.2 million above 2022's, and Democratic-primary voters are far closer to Republican-primary voters than 2022's 400,000 Republican lead
signals.value: Texas Tribune (Nov 1, preliminary): more than 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% turnout, past 2018's record; 2022's early vote was 5.5 million (31%), 2024's 9 million (49%). Secretary of State count as of Oct 30: 7,410,631, 38.92% of 19,041,684 registered (CBS Texas). theoelections (Oct 30): 7,744,549 ballots, 7,463,553 in person and 280,996 by mail; Democratic-primary-only voters 2,100,396 (28.1%) of in-person ballots, Republican-primary-only 2,238,247 (30.0%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%); mail 32.8% Democratic-only to 26.2% Republican-only. At the same point in 2022 Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 (Derek Ryan via NBC 5, Oct 27).
signals.catch: No party registration: 'party' is primary history, 39% of in-person voters have none, and 2022's electorate was unusually Republican. Republican-primary voters won the closing days and finished ahead in person (the separate signal). Mark Jones: 'definitely high turnout'; Matt Angle (Democratic strategist): 'That doesn't mean Democrats are going to win.'
signals.src: Texas Tribune via KSAT, Nov 1; CBS Texas, Oct 31; theoelections, Oct 30; NBC 5 DFW, Oct 27
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlets and official data; theoelections is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Texas's Republican close: Republican-primary voters finished ahead of Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots, 2,238,247 to 2,100,396, after trailing through the first week
signals.value: theoelections (as of Oct 30, the final day): in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 2,238,247 (30.0%) against Democratic-primary-only 2,100,396 (28.1%), both 185,982 (2.5%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%), on 7,463,553 in-person ballots; the Oct 28 count had Republicans ahead 1,757,395 to 1,699,975 and the Oct 29 count 1,905,771 to 1,824,245. Mail: 92,275 Democratic-only (32.8%) to 73,688 Republican-only (26.2%). Ryan's statewide Democratic-primary edge had fallen from about 115,000 after the first week to nearly 57,000 through Oct 28 (NBC 5; CBS Texas).
signals.catch: Primary history is not vote choice, and 39% of in-person voters have none. Against 2022, when Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 at this point, the electorate is still far more Democratic; the signal is the direction of the final days.
signals.src: theoelections, Oct 30; CBS Texas, Oct 29; NBC 5 DFW, Oct 27
signals.aff: theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Florida's early vote ended R+2.5 in the Nov 1 file, with Republicans up 287,000 in person and the lead growing every day of the final week
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Nov 1 (the app's official panel): 3,465,546 in-person ballots, 1,497,201 Republican to 1,209,843 Democratic (R+287,358); 1,937,212 mail ballots returned, 830,632 Democratic to 677,817 Republican (D+152,815); combined 40.3% Republican to 37.8% Democratic on 5,402,758 ballots, from R+1.8 on Oct 29, R+1.0 on Oct 27 and D+6.7 at twenty days out. Bay News 9 (Nov 2): just under 5.2 million ballots at Sunday's close, nearly 300,000 more than 2022's same point, almost 1.4 million of them Friday through Sunday; Republicans more than 1.4 million in person and just over 668,000 by mail, Democrats just over 1.1 million in person and more than 800,000 by mail.
signals.catch: The same-point comparison still favors Democrats: R+6.2 at two days out in 2022 and R+10.6 in 2024 (the app's official panel), and 2022's final early vote was R+6.4. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in both years; the outstanding mail is Democratic-leaning. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Nov 1; Bay News 9, Nov 2
signals.aff: Official data; Bay News 9 is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail returns finished early voting 5% behind 2022's same point, with Democrats' returns down 12% and Republicans' up 14%
signals.value: Call the Map (state file through Oct 31): 1,053,168 mail ballots returned, 13,545 that day, 5% fewer than the same point in 2022; Democrats 681,934 (about 65%, down 12% from 771,898), Republicans 265,272 (about 25%, up 14% from 233,284), unaffiliated and other 105,962 (up 4%); D+39.6 against D+48.6 at the same point in 2022 and D+22.7 in 2024. Philadelphia 95,108 (D+80.5), Allegheny 129,648 (D+56.0), Montgomery 94,771 (D+47.5), Bucks 85,926 (D+28.9). The state's Nov 1 file: 1,056,549 returned of 1,297,730 requested; the app's official panel reads D+39.5 against D+48.6 in 2022 and D+23.0 in 2024.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+48.6 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national vote), and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting; the state has no in-person early voting, so there is no in-person count to offset it. Call the Map notes 2022's file counted every ballot with a return date. The official comparison is on the app's panel, so this signal is the turnout picture only. About 241,000 approved ballots were still outstanding.
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file

signals.title: Arizona's early ballots are R+12,335 (0.8 points) by registration on 1.60 million through Nov 1, with Maricopa R+5,314 and Pima D+55,007
signals.value: Go Right Strategies' county compilation (Nov 1, 11:52 a.m. ET): 1,602,707 ballots returned, Republicans 609,283 (38.0%), Democrats 596,948 (37.2%), other 396,476 (24.7%), R+12,335; Maricopa (updated Oct 30) 930,818 at R+5,314; Pima 279,920 at D+55,007; the lead was R+13,526 on Oct 29 and R+11,514 on Oct 27. Call the Map: R+0.8 on about 1.60 million. The app's panel reads R+0.8 on 1,602,837 ballots in the Nov 1 file against R+8.4 at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice: Republicans have a registration edge near 300,000, so a lead this small means Democrats are returning ballots at a higher rate; there is no official statewide daily file, the compilation is from county reports with Maricopa two days stale, and the app has no 2022 same-point baseline. The tracker is a Republican consulting firm.
signals.src: Go Right Strategies, Nov 1; Call the Map, Nov 1
signals.aff: Go Right Strategies is a Republican consulting firm; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Wisconsin's absentee returns are about 50,000 ahead of 2022's same point, but mail returns are down more than 20% while in-person absentees are up more than 50%, most in Republican Washington and Waukesha counties
signals.value: WPR (Oct 31, Elections Commission data as of Oct 30): 693,334 absentee ballots returned, 'about 50,000 more than at the same point in 2022'; mail about 300,000 against about 384,000 in 2022 (down more than 20%), in-person about 394,000 against about 259,000 (up more than 50%); Milwaukee's mail down more than 25% and in-person up 45%, Dane's mail down more than 30% and in-person up about 50%, Washington's in-person up about 75%, Waukesha's up more than 40%. Dairyland Sentinel (Oct 27 file): 513,602 against 503,180 (+2.1%), with Milwaukee down 1.9% and Dane down 6.9% while Waukesha was up 7.9% and Washington 30%.
signals.catch: No party registration, so this is turnout only, and both parties pushed voters away from mail; the Democratic counties' totals have been closing the gap as in-person voting ran through Nov 1. Handrick: 'While the early returns are encouraging for the GOP, they are not predictive.'
signals.src: WPR (Avery Martinez) via Urban Milwaukee, Oct 31; Dairyland Sentinel (Joe Handrick), Oct 27
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; the Dairyland Sentinel analysis is on a conservative-leaning site by a former Republican legislator

signals.title: Michigan passed 1.8 million ballots by Friday, with 358,000 early in-person votes that did not exist in 2022 and absentee returns past 2022's same-point figure
signals.value: AP (Nov 1): more than 1.8 million Michiganders had voted as of Friday Oct 30. CBS News Detroit (Oct 30, Secretary of State dashboard): more than 1.3 million absentee ballots returned and more than 358,000 early in-person ballots, of more than 7.4 million active registered voters; Detroit's clerk projects 40-45% turnout against 34% in 2022. The Secretary of State's Oct 27 release: 1,176,375 absentee ballots returned against 1,126,246 a week before Election Day 2022.
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction, and the department cautions that higher early numbers 'do not necessarily mean' higher overall turnout. Early in-person voting ended Nov 1; the final count was not published by Monday morning.
signals.src: AP via PBS NewsHour, Nov 1; CBS News Detroit (Hannah McIlree), Oct 30; Michigan Secretary of State, Oct 27

signals.title: Maine's absentee returns are 36% ahead of 2022 at the same point (275,563 against about 202,000), and Democrats are about half of them
signals.value: Secretary of State figures as of Thursday Oct 29 (WGME): 313,611 absentee ballots requested, 312,874 issued, 275,563 returned and accepted, 'more than 276,000' against 'more than 202,000' at this point in 2022; a return rate above 88% against almost 81%; more than 152,000 cast in the presence of a clerk; Secretary Bellows: 'We are seeing the requests and the returns way up over the last midterm election in 2022.' Press Herald (Oct 28, data through Oct 27): nearly 222,000 accepted, 32% above 2022's same point and 20% below 2024's; about half of voters so far are Democrats (36% of registered Democrats have voted), Republicans about 22% of returns (18% of registered Republicans), unaffiliated more than a quarter; in the 2nd District Republicans are 27% of early votes against 33% at this point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice, and against 2022 the party gap is about a point narrower (Call the Map's Oct 26 reading: D+27.8 against D+28.7), so the Democratic reading comes from turnout and the 2024 comparison; unaffiliated voters decide the Collins race. In-person absentee voting ended Oct 29.
signals.src: WGME (Allyson LaPierre), Oct 29; Portland Press Herald (Ethan Horton), Oct 28

signals.title: Nevada's statewide in-person vote finished Republican (R+8,674 in the Oct 31 file), and mail is 58% of the total
signals.value: The state's Oct 31 file (the app's official panel): in-person ballots statewide 121,631 Republican to 112,957 Democratic (R+8,674) on 308,019, mail 173,201 Democratic to 119,102 Republican (D+54,099) on 410,884. Ralston (Nov 1): mail is 58 percent of the statewide total and Clark's mail margin is 'close to 2-to-1'; rurals R+30,000. Erik Jimenez's count (Oct 31): about 135,800 Republican 2022 voters had not yet voted, against 75.1% of 2022's Democrats already in.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which the county-wide figures absorb (Clark overall is near D+66,000 against about 24,000 at this point in 2022); the in-person lead is small on 308,000 ballots. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 31); Nevada Independent, Nov 1
signals.aff: Secretary of State data; Ralston is a nonpartisan journalist

signals.title: Call the Map: the registered-party gap moved toward Republicans in three of the five states comparable day by day with 2022, and Republican turnout has run near 2022's
signals.value: Call the Map (Nov 1): 51,430,902 ballots in 47 states; the five states comparable with 2022 by day (North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Maine, Nevada and Florida) are up 14% together, four of five ahead of 2022's pace, and 'the registered party gap moved toward Republicans' in Pennsylvania (D+48.6 to D+39.6), Maine (D+25.9 to D+24.3) and Nevada's Clark mail (D+23.5 to D+20.6), toward Democrats in North Carolina (D+6.8 to D+12.2) and Florida (R+6.7 to R+2.8). Newsweek (Oct 31, UF Election Lab): in the party-registration states, Democrats 43%, Republicans 32%, others 25%.
signals.catch: Three of the five moves are in mail-only or mail-heavy counts where Democrats are shifting to in person, and the national 43-32 split covers only the 27 states with party registration. Democrats' 2022 early-vote edge preceded a national vote they lost by about 3 points, which is why the edge alone says little.
signals.src: Call the Map, Nov 1; Newsweek (Hugh Cameron), Oct 31
signals.aff: Call the Map is an independent tracker; UF Election Lab is nonpartisan

signals.title: A record 54.5 million have voted, past 2022's 45.9 million, with turnout gains concentrated among Black, Hispanic and young voters and voters who skipped 2022
signals.value: UF Election Lab: 54,467,368 ballots in the app's Nov 2 file (49 jurisdictions; 24.4 million by mail, 30.1 million in person) against 45,920,446 in all of 2022. Newsweek (Oct 31): about 49.6 million by Friday, Democrats 43% and Republicans 32% of ballots in party-registration states; the AP found Texas's early vote up 50% on 2022 and South Carolina's up 83%. Georgia's Black share is 32.4% against 30.2% at this point in 2022 (AJC); North Carolina's Black voters cast 1.5 times 2022's ballots and voters 18-25 nearly doubled (WBTV); G. Elliott Morris (L2 data, Oct 30): North Carolina Democrats cast 74.6% of two-party early ballots among voters with no 2022 vote, against 58.0% at the same point in 2022.
signals.catch: Turnout is not vote choice, and Election Day was Republican in 2022; the national party split covers only the registration states, and Morris's figures are L2's modeled two-party split in a state that does register party. DDHQ's Skelley: 'we must be careful not to divine with certainty winners and losers from the entrails of AB/EV data.'
signals.src: UF Election Lab, Nov 2; Newsweek, Oct 31; AJC, Oct 31; WBTV, Nov 1; G. Elliott Morris, Oct 30
signals.aff: UF Election Lab is nonpartisan; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Morris is an independent analyst
